chapter_theme: The close of Suramanjari's ilampakam: the first nights of Civakan and Suramanjari, her jealous sulk over the painted figure ended when he lays his head on her anklets as her old vow required, his leave-taking, and his secret homecoming to his foster parents and wives, Gunamalai blaming her own deeds and he crediting her penance, before he leaves the city again as a merchant.

2081.reading: Her hot breasts, like the joined tusks of an elephant that has battered a golden hill, steeped in southern sandal and swelling under their strings of pearls, redden at their gem tips as he drinks her old beauty, and he is like those who have entered heaven.
2081.nuance: The beauty he drinks is தொன்னலம், her beauty of long standing: the woman who had vowed to look on no man has kept it unspent until now.
2081.event: Civakan and Suramanjari come together on their first night.

2082.reading: The hero's chest and the girl's breasts make war and revel; the beat of the anklets, the clinking girdle and the drum-like rhythm mingle, her braided hair moans, and he lingers so that he cannot leave the flower bed.
2082.nuance: Love-making is told in the vocabulary of battle (செரு, போர்), with the ornaments as the war-drums.

2083.reading: Drinking wine from a gem cup until drowsiness came on, he gave her a fresh blue lily with one hand, and thinking that if the golden doe came close her slender waist would be hurt, he held her with his two shoulders.
2083.event: Civakan gives Suramanjari a lily and embraces her.

2084.reading: She sulks and pulls away, telling him not to embrace her with a chest that many embrace as they do the broad Ganges; he, in distress, saying he has done no wrong and asking the jasmine-garlanded one not to be angry, worships her small red-dyed feet.
2084.nuance: The charge has a literal base in this epic: by this ilampakam the hero has already married several wives, so her figure of the river all may bathe in is a complaint as well as a lover's pretext.
2084.event: Suramanjari, jealous, refuses Civakan's embrace, and he bows to her feet.

2085.reading: She asks whether he was not delighting in gazing at the painted figure, and he answers the slim-waisted one that she stood pressed to the wall so that her form showed on it, and his eye, taking it for her, the beautiful maid, clung to it.
2085.nuance: The construal of line 2 is uncertain: it may be his excuse (she leaned on the wall and her likeness showed there) or part of her charge (he stood fixed at the wall); the reading here takes it as his reply, closed by என்றான்.
2085.event: Suramanjari accuses Civakan of gazing at a painted figure; he says he took it for her.

2086.reading: Her fine silk slipping and the gems on her waist flashing, hurt, she narrowed her eyes, glared at him in love's anger, and with earrings shining and her garland coming loose with her hair, the bright-bangled one stood sulking like a flowering branch of bright gems.
2086.event: Suramanjari stands apart in her sulk.

2087.reading: She says she saw him come as an old man singing and sit in her lower chamber, and saw him sit unblinking gazing at the painted figure, and cries away with this love, the one town has become two; and the tears she wept split the young man's life.
2087.nuance: She now knows the old singer who sat in her chamber was Civakan in disguise. The phrase ஓரூர் இரண்டஃகமாயிற்று (the one town has become two, or two measures) seems proverbial for a divided love, but its exact sense is not clear from the verse.
2087.event: Suramanjari recalls Civakan's disguise as an old man and his gazing at the painting, and weeps.

2088.reading: Setting his head on the anklets of her small red feet so that his garland came undone, and saying that the great bear without complaint the wrongs the small have done, the young man ended the sulk of the woman with spear-bright eyes.
2088.nuance: He has just said he did no wrong (2084), yet he pleads as the small one who erred, making her the great one who forgives: the maxim is used as a lover's tactic. The gesture also completes her vow of 899, that she would keep apart until he came defeated and worshipped her anklet feet.
2088.event: Civakan lays his head on Suramanjari's anklets and ends her sulk.

claims.claim: the great bear without complaint the wrongs done by the small

2089.reading: Ending the sulk of her whose speech outdoes the yal and is sweeter than nectar, and tasting the ripe fruit of love that has no hard stone, the man with the hanging garland did not leave his play with the girl, and was like the moon and sun joined in one when their time comes round.
2089.nuance: ஊழ் here is the turn of time that brings sun and moon together at the new moon, not deeds of a former birth.
2089.event: After the quarrel Civakan and Suramanjari are reunited in love.

2090.reading: Kama, holding bow and arrow, guards this doorway, drinking the laughing face and smile of the woman whose waist shines with green silk, pearls and coral, and watching for desire and signs, his only work to shoot.
2090.nuance: The god of love is posted as doorkeeper of their chamber, where earlier her father's guards had kept men out.

2091.reading: He set ornaments in her ears, crowned her braid with a strung garland whose scent carried far, put pearl-tipped bands on her soft arms, painted her body with sandal, stroked the gold girdle on her waist and set her bright bangles right.

2092.reading: On the couch fragrant with soft smoke from tagara wood of the hill of white falls, with fine agil, honey and sugar mixed and burned to end loneliness, the youth like a king of beasts said this to the white-bangled girl.
2092.event: Civakan prepares to speak to Suramanjari on the couch.

2093.reading: He tells the carp-eyed girl not to worry about his business, for he will be parted from her only a few days and her duty is to bear her rare beauty; she answers that she wants nothing but what he wants, that she has gone with one mind into his heart, and what pleases him is what pleases her.
2093.nuance: The verse holds both voices: lines 1 and 2 are his, lines 3 and 4 hers. The woman who had sworn to shun all men now defines her will as his.
2093.event: Civakan tells Suramanjari he must leave for a few days, and she consents.

claims.claim: a wife wants nothing other than what her husband wants, and his joy is her joy

2094.reading: Hearing her honey-sweet words woven with modesty, he embraced her so that his ornaments left their marks, told the honey-garlanded one not to pine and let her beauty fade, rose, and went with his sword-bearing friends round him gladly into his own house.
2094.event: Civakan leaves Suramanjari and goes with his friends to his foster father's house.

2095.reading: He ended the wasting of his mother, who, looking at horses, elephants and tall golden chariots, never ceasing night or day to cry where is my son, had washed her hands in the tears she wept and grieved like a wax figure taken by fire.
2095.nuance: The mother scans the horses, elephants and chariots, the things her son rode, as if they could tell her where he is.
2095.event: Civakan returns to his foster mother and ends her grief.

2096.reading: So that not even spies should know, they silenced their speech and wanted to tell the kin by gestures; the kin gathered and embraced him, beat themselves, wilted, and crying Nambi, o Nambi, wept tears that ran down and washed his feet.
2096.nuance: His return must stay hidden from Kattiyangaran's spies: even the reunion is held in signs.
2096.event: Civakan's kin greet him in secret, weeping, without words.

2097.reading: When Kandukkan rebuked them the uproar fell still like the waves of the roaring sea, and thinking the secret would get out, he proclaimed in the city that today was the day his father died, and all were cooled within by a joy without end.
2097.nuance: The weeping of joy is given out as mourning so that no spy guesses its cause. The verse is read here with கந்துகண் as Kantukkatan and எந்தை as his father; both are the likeliest readings, not certain.
2097.event: Kantukkatan quiets the kin and announces a death anniversary to explain the weeping.

2098.reading: Tattai of the red carp-like eyes, rejoicing, begged him in sweet words to go and see her younger sister, and in auspicious fashion he set a garland of unceasing honey and a fragrant wreath on her and painted her with saffron.
2098.nuance: எங்கை, my younger sister, is Gunamalai, called so by her co-wife. Whether the woman he adorns in lines 3 and 4 is Tattai, before he goes, or Gunamalai on his arrival is not clear from the verse.
2098.event: Gandharvadattai sends Civakan to see Gunamalai, and he adorns a wife with garland and saffron.

2099.reading: Gunamalai cries do not touch sinful me, lord, there is no need, I am a wrongdoer, and grieves, weeps and melts; he tells the girl with lily eyes not to grieve at all, for all his survival came from her penance, the girl whose body smells of musk.
2099.nuance: She calls herself தீவினை உடைய, one with evil deeds, because his seizure followed his rescue of her from the elephant; he turns her guilt into merit. The verse does not name a school for the power of தவம்.
2099.event: Gunamalai blames herself for Civakan's danger; he says her penance saved him.

claims.claim: a wife's penance can preserve her husband's life

2100.reading: He tells her that though her soft gait like a swan's, her look, her grace, her jewels, her beauty, her lightning-slim waist, her breasts and her face were painted in his mind, the day he was parted from her was like an aeon.
2100.nuance: Her image painted in his mind did not make the parting short: memory is set against absence and loses.

2101.reading: Telling the young woman things to delight her, he slept, and the next day he gave all the wealth he had gained to his father, and with his kin around him, as a merchant on a fine horse, the man of the flawless garland left his city.
2101.nuance: வாமான் வாணிகனாகி may mean he went as a horse-trader or simply rode as a merchant; either way he leaves in disguise, still hidden from the usurper.
2101.event: Civakan gives his gains to Kantukkatan and leaves the city in a merchant's guise.

links.note: Suramanjari vowed in 899 to keep apart until Civakan came defeated (தோற்று) and worshipped her anklet feet; in 2088 he lays his head on her anklets and her sulk ends.
links.teaches: Her vow is kept not by a defeat he admits but by a lover's bow inside a quarrel he says he did not cause, so the pride that began in a contest is satisfied by the rites of love.

links.note: The Kural says the loser of a lovers' quarrel is the winner, as union shows; Civakan casts himself as the small one who erred, yields, and wins her.
links.teaches: The epic gives the couplet's paradox a plot: a woman who swore to see the man defeated gets his surrender, and his surrender is exactly what wins him her.

gains.a: the hero's bow at her feet reads as a known strategy of oodal rather than humiliation
gains.b: the couplet's abstract loser and winner become a named pair whose defeat had been sworn as a vow

links.note: Naladiyar 77 says the great bear faults hard to bear, which is why their friendship is sought; Civakan uses the same maxim to plead with a sulking wife after denying any fault.
links.teaches: A maxim about the forbearance of the great in friendship turns, in a lover's mouth, into flattery that makes the angry woman the great one and so obliges her to forgive.

gains.a: the hero's maxim is seen to be a borrowed rule of friendship pressed into love's service
gains.b: the quatrain's rule is shown working as rhetoric: naming someone great lays on them the duty to forbear

links.note: In Kural 1311 the woman refuses his chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; Suramanjari refuses a chest many embrace like the Ganges.
links.teaches: The Kural's sulking pretext is that other women merely look at him, but in a polygamous epic where the hero has already married several wives the same refusal names a fact.

gains.a: Suramanjari's complaint is placed in the oodal convention, so it reads as play that leads to reunion
gains.b: the couplet's mock charge is seen with a literal referent, which shows how close the convention runs to real grievance

links.note: In Kural 1320 she is angry even at his gaze, asking whom he thinks of; here she is angry at his gaze on a painted figure, and he claims he took the picture for her.
links.teaches: The epic supplies the object the couplet leaves imagined, a painted woman on the wall, and turns the lover's defence round: his gaze was faithful because he mistook the picture for her.

gains.a: the epic scene inherits a precise oodal type, the jealousy of the gaze
gains.b: the couplet's suspicion gets a concrete rival and an answer the man can give, which it never offers

links.note: Kural 1269 says one day is like seven to those waiting for the absent one's return; Civakan tells Gunamalai the day he was parted from her was like an aeon.
links.teaches: The epic moves the measure of absence from the waiting woman to the returned man and inflates it from seven days to an aeon, said only once the parting is over and as a gift of words.

gains.a: Civakan's hyperbole is placed in the Kural's tradition of time stretched by longing
gains.b: the couplet's longing, which commentators argue about assigning to the man, is here plainly spoken by a man to the wife he left

links.note: The sage foretold that Civakan would be seized, carried off by a yaksha, and seen again after some days; in 2095 he comes home and his mother's grief ends.
links.teaches: The prophecy promised only that he would be seen again, and the return shows its cost: the mother was comforted by the word yet still wept herself thin until he stood before her.

links.note: In 1132 Gunamalai, near death with grief, clung to the sage's words as a raft; in 2099 Civakan says he survived by her penance.
links.teaches: The grief that the narrator showed Gunamalai surviving by holding to a prophecy is renamed by the hero as தவம், so her endurance becomes the cause of his rescue rather than only her consolation.

source_issues: Every verse except 2084 was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2087 line 3 ஓரூ ரிரண்டஃக மாயிற் is obscure as divided; the sense of the proverb is not certain.
2097 line 1 கந்துகண் கழற is read as Kantukkatan's name in short form; the division is not certain.
2089 line 1 prints னழிழ்துறழ், apparently a misprint for னமிழ்துறழ் (அமிழ்து உறழ், like nectar).

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, called சீவகசாமி in the invocation
a merchant's daughter who loses the scented-powder contest and shuns men, now Civakan's wife
the god of love, lord of the five arrows, who brings spring
Kandukkatan's wife, Civakan's foster mother (named in 365)
Civakan's kin in the old city
the merchant who takes up and raises the newborn Civakan
daughter of the Vidyadhara king, defeated by Civakan at the vina; his wife, called தத்தை
a merchant's daughter, Suramanjari's rival in the powder contest, whom Civakan saves and marries
